strengths: Provides a controlled modular study that freezes the LD-FPG encoder-decoder and swaps only the latent propagator, which helps isolate propagator effects.

Evaluates several systems of increasing complexity, including alanine dipeptide, 7JFL, HIV-1 protease, A1AR, and A2AR, with multiple metrics such as dihedral JSD, contact correlation, IDDT/RMSD stability, and TICA timescales.

Reports a plausible and potentially useful empirical trade-off: the autoregressive NN is most stable for long rollouts, score-guided Langevin can better recover side-chain rotamer distributions when the score is good, and Koopman is a lightweight but overly damped baseline.
Includes supplementary ablations on encoder width, pooling size, data efficiency, temporal stride, architecture, and runtime, which improves transparency compared with many purely qualitative papers.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: GLDP is not a new simulation method but a comparison of existing propagators (DMD/Koopman, MLP autoregression, score-guided Langevin) inside an already-pretrained LD-FPG latent space. The main contribution is empirical benchmarking rather than a methodological advance.

The kinetic evaluation is not convincing. Langevin is an equilibrium sampler with arbitrary latent temperature, time step, and sampling stride, calibrated only to match short-horizon RMSD-per-frame. Its TICA timescale in SDE steps is not physically comparable to MD or to the other propagators, yet the paper reports these values in kinetic comparisons and claims coherent timescales.

There is a conceptual mismatch in comparing score-guided Langevin with autoregressive/Koopman propagators for dynamics. Langevin is used to sample the static equilibrium score, not to learn a transition operator, so it cannot be expected to reproduce temporal kinetics; the paper acknowledges no exact physical kinetics in places but still advances kinetic claims.

Benchmarks in Table 1 lack sufficient fairness and detail. It is unclear whether LSS, MD-Gen, and GeoTDM were trained/evaluated with identical preprocessing, data splits, temporal strides, and latent dimensions. Several entries are N/A, error bars are missing, and only GLDP-NN is compared rather than the full GLDP propagator set.

Quantitative comparison of the three propagators is narrow: Table 2 focuses only on ADP and A1AR dihedral JSD, while A2AR activation-surface results are largely qualitative. There is no systematic TICA, contact-map, or stability comparison for all propagators across all systems.

The claim of being the first learned all-atom rollout to recover a GPCR activation surface is not quantitatively supported. A2AR results are shown as visual density contours and 1D projections without free-energy differences, barrier estimates, JSDs, or direct baseline comparisons on A2AR.

Long-horizon stability relies on an arbitrary IDDT threshold of 0.65 with no sensitivity analysis. Failure times may be sensitive to this threshold, the reference initial frame, and the noise calibration, making the stability rankings less robust than presented.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The manuscript mentions an anonymous repository but no accessible link appears in the supplied text, and many system-specific choices, such as temperature, step size, score clipping, and per-system calibration, are tuned by protocols that are not standardized across systems.

strengths: Provides a controlled comparison of three propagator families (Koopman/DMD, autoregressive MLP, score-guided Langevin) within a fixed, pre-trained LD-FPG latent space, which is a reasonable way to isolate the effect of the propagation rule.

Evaluates on a hierarchy of systems (alanine dipeptide, 7JFL, HIV-1 protease, A1AR/A2AR), including large membrane proteins, and reports multiple complementary metrics: structural JSD, contact-map correlation, IDDT stability, TICA timescales, and dihedral free-energy surfaces.
Includes useful ablation studies in the appendix (encoder width, pooling size, denoiser/Langevin settings, data efficiency, frame skipping, residual vs direct prediction, computational timing).
Offers practical discussion of trade-offs: autoregressive NN for stability, Langevin for side-chain rotamers, Koopman as a lightweight but rigid baseline.
Reproducibility is explicitly considered, with code-release intentions, fixed seeds, environment details, and extensive implementation hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper introduces no substantially new model or algorithm. GLDP is essentially a wrapper that swaps standard propagators into an already-published LD-FPG encoder-decoder, so the contribution is mainly an empirical comparison rather than a new capability for top-tier AI.

The central dynamic claims are not adequately supported. The paper repeatedly discusses kinetics and 'physical timescales', but times are reported in arbitrary simulation steps with no wall-clock or physical-time calibration. The authors acknowledge this, then still claim coherent physical kinetics; this is contradictory.

The TICA timescale comparison is weak: GLDP remains far from ground truth on several systems (e.g., 1R6W TICA 980 vs 1670; A1AR 650 vs 1059), yet it is presented as recovering kinetics. No lag-time sensitivity or uncertainty is reported for TICA, and step counts are not comparable across propagators with different strides.

The benchmark comparison is potentially confounded. Only GLDP-NN is compared to external baselines in Table 1, while the other two GLDP propagators are not; moreover, GLDP inherits the LD-FPG encoder-decoder, whereas baselines use their own architectures, so model-level comparisons do not cleanly isolate the propagator.

The A2AR GPCR activation result is mostly qualitative and lacks external baselines. The claim of a 'first learned, all-atom rollout' recovering an activation surface is not well supported without comparison to prior generative trajectory models or quantitative free-energy errors.

Baseline treatment is uneven. LSS is reported as unstable on A1AR, but no diagnostic is given to establish whether this is an inherent limitation or an implementation/tuning issue. Koopman is implemented as a simple truncated DMD linear map, which may be a strawman compared with modern deep Koopman methods.

Evaluation metrics lack sufficient rigor in places: Table 1 reports no error bars for key metrics, baseline hyperparameter tuning is not described, and the IDDT failure threshold (0.65) is described as empirically calibrated but not systematically validated.

The claim that freezing the decoder 'enforces local geometric validity' and decouples propagation from high-frequency physics is plausible but not fully tested. It may also make stability comparisons depend strongly on the latent geometry rather than the propagator itself.

Some presentation and reproducibility issues remain: missing code link in the appendix/statement, inconsistent system naming, typographical errors, and incomplete specification of some MD preprocessing/thermostat/barostat details.

strengths: The paper performs a controlled comparison by holding the LD-FPG encoder-decoder fixed and swapping only the latent propagator, which helps isolate the effect of the propagation rule from representation quality.

It implements and evaluates three representative propagator families—Koopman/DMD, autoregressive MLP, and score-guided Langevin—within a unified framework and across several protein systems ranging from alanine dipeptide to GPCRs.

The empirical findings provide some useful practical guidance: the autoregressive NN tends to be most stable for long rollouts, score-guided Langevin can recover side-chain rotamer statistics when the score is well learned, and Koopman offers a lightweight but rigid baseline.
The appendix is detailed, with algorithms, notation, hyperparameter tables, ablations, and a glossary, showing a serious attempt at transparency and reproducibility.
The A2AR activation-surface visualization is an interesting qualitative demonstration that latent propagators can access functionally relevant GPCR conformational regions.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited for a top-tier AI conference: the paper mainly benchmarks existing propagator classes inside an existing LD-FPG latent space, and 'GLDP' is largely an integration wrapper rather than a new method.

The main quantitative comparison in Table 1 is incomplete and not fully fair: it compares only GLDP-NN against LSS/MD-Gen/GeoTDM, not all three propagators; several systems lack error bars or statistical tests; and A2AR is evaluated only qualitatively without external baselines.

Kinetic claims are overstated. TICA timescales are reported in steps and explicitly not calibrated to physical time, yet the abstract and text claim coherent physical timescales. There is no lag-time convergence, Markov state model validation, or wall-clock mapping to MD.

Langevin hyperparameters are ad hoc and system-dependent. The early failure on alanine dipeptide appears to result from an aggressive step size chosen by an RMSD-matching heuristic rather than an inherent limitation of score-guided Langevin, weakening the conclusion that it is unstable.

The 'autoregressive neural network' class is represented only by a simple MLP. Stronger sequence models such as LSTMs, transformers, neural ODEs/SDEs, or equivariant models are discussed but not compared, so the comparison across propagator classes is incomplete.

The score-guided Langevin propagator uses a static equilibrium score, not a transition operator, and integrates no momenta; the paper acknowledges this but still makes dynamical/fidelity claims that go beyond what is demonstrated.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing/blank code links and heavy reliance on external datasets and the LD-FPG model. Simulation conditions such as force field, thermostat/barostat, temperature, and pressure are deferred to prior work rather than fully specified.

The scope and significance for the AI community are unclear: the method is system-specific, does not demonstrate transferability, and does not show a clear computational advantage over MD or enhanced sampling beyond qualitative latent rollouts.

Some metrics are weakly defined or coarse: JSD over high-dimensional coordinates is not clearly specified, contact-map correlation is a time-averaged structural proxy rather than a dynamical metric, and there are minor inconsistencies such as 'GLDP' vs. 'GLDP-NN' labeling and differing failure-time numbers between sections.

The title and abstract overclaim by suggesting simulation of all-atom protein dynamics in physical time, whereas the method propagates in a learned latent space with a frozen decoder and explicitly provides no exact physical kinetics.
